title: The Paradox of Welcoming the Executioner
english: Just as Thomas went to the Indians, Peter to the Romans, John to the Asiatics, and Paul declared he had preached from Jerusalem and as far as Illyricum, so each herald carried the message to their own people, proclaiming Christ and the mysteries that came from him and were accomplished through him.
But the Jews, burning with zeal and anger and being pierced, could no longer endure the widespread testimony of Longinus, which had already spread through the land in many ways.

Therefore they persuaded Pilate to write falsely to Caesar about the blessed Longinus, claiming that he held alien thoughts toward the Roman Empire, had abandoned his weapons, and was proclaiming Christ as king to the nations.
By these very words, he had already filled his own homeland and country with such teachings.
Moreover, they sent along these letters money and accused Longinus of a capital offense, having seized the attention of Caesar himself, for his sake.
Imperial letters were then sent into Judea to Pilate, bearing instructions according to Longinus and those associated with him.
These orders directed that those who had neglected their weapons should take up swords and behead their targets.
Pilate, with great zeal, entrusted the execution of these Caesar’s letters to the officers overseeing the murders.
They swiftly crossed the land of the Cappadocians, arrived, and learned that in a paternal field Longinus was philosophizing and practicing quietness, having withdrawn from all political affairs.
Quietly they seized his field, intending to carry out the decree of Pilate and of Caesar, so that Longinus would not be driven into flight.
Thus they suddenly stood against the man, as if they had crossed some other threshold, and none of those with them dared to lay a hand on anything.
Then entering and happening upon Longinus, not knowing that he is the one sought by them and by Pilate, they begin to ask where Longinus is.
But he, the divine Spirit having foreshadowed the drama for him, says: 'Follow me,' and I point him out to you.

Then the blessed one, as is fitting, rejoicing and eager for the martyr’s sacrifice, said: 'How beautiful are the feet of those who proclaim peace, of those who proclaim good things (Isaiah 52:7, Romans 10:15).'
Now I will see the heavens opened, now I will recount the glory of the Father, now I will behold the ineffable flash of the Spirit.
Now I will say, 'Lord Jesus Christ, receive my spirit (Psalm 31:5, Luke 23:46)', as Stephen the first of the martyrs, whose most radiant voice I have heard.

Now Jerusalem, the heavenly golden tower, the same indeed the homeland of the angels, and indeed the metropolis of the whole choir of the holy, with rattles, triumphs, and royal trophies, I will ascend.
Now I put off the clay tunic and the many-groaning bonds of the flesh, I lay aside and free myself from corruption.
For I am drawn to incorruption, having a life free of winter’s storm going out from the temporary life, of which many are the waves and grievous the shipwrecks.
A solitary haven is that immortal life, wherein the saints dwell.
Be glad, O soul, turn toward your Maker as you depart; show a joyful countenance at the time when the face is called beautiful.
Let us kindly entertain those who bring us such great blessings, rejoicing as we do so, and let us set forth a richly laden table for those who summon us to the royal dinner.
Having spoken these words to himself, Longinus welcomed those who had come to him into his own house.
He entertained them splendidly, with a cheerful face and exceeding joy, and having eaten together with them at the table he had prepared, he began to ask them after the meal what they needed.

But they, having exacted oaths from him that he would not make public what concerned them nor reveal the bold mystery, then declared the writings sent against Pilate from Caesar, and said that Longinus, together with two others, had met and severed the head.

And Longinus, inquiring who these were that were with him at the same time, came to know that they were indeed the ones who had hired the Jewish servant and had preferred the Christ, and so he wrote to them with great earnestness, urging them to come quickly to him to share in great blessings.
Longinus entertained them for one day and then a second; on the third day he took them into a field, where he awaited those who had been sent out from him.
But having learned that he was near, he announced to them, saying, 'I myself am Longinus, the one you have been seeking.'
But they at first did not believe him; yet after this they were persuaded and wept, pulling out their own hairs and speaking with mournful voices toward Longinus.
What was your undertaking, my friend, that seemed good?
What was your purpose in bringing violence upon those who came to you, leading to slaughter in your own house?
Why did you prepare a feast for those who came intending your slaughter and remained to carry it out?
translator_notes: The Greek text contains edge fragments at the beginning and end of the chunk, but no mid-word cuts are present; all clauses are complete enough for literal translation.
The phrase καὶ ἄλλος ἄλλοις is rendered idiomatically as 'each herald carried the message to their own people' to avoid mechanical repetition while preserving the sense of distributive proclamation.
The verb ἐν ἀγρῷ πατρῴῳ τὸν Λογγῖνον φιλοσοφεῖν is a present infinitive construction indicating ongoing action; translated as 'Longinus was philosophizing' to reflect the contemporaneous context.
The expression τὸ ἐπίταγμα Πιλάτου καὶ Καί σαρος ἐπιτελέσαι βουλόμενοι is rendered as 'intending to carry out the decree of Pilate and of Caesar' to clarify the purpose behind seizing the field.
The final clause in the source text ends mid-phrase with 'δεῖπνον' (no closing word or punctuation).

The phrase 'παραγενο μένοις' appears to be a scribal error or corruption for 'παραγενομένων' (having come), but as per instructions, I do not invent or correct the Greek; I translate the given letters literally as fragments.
baehrens: PG 93; Homilia i in sanctum Longinum centurionem (Khazarzar) u01 rem early

title: Martyrdom of Longinus
english: You have prepared and set a table for me, not just for one day, but also for a second and third day.
Have you not seen in your blood, which is sought by us, the wine?
Now, what is there to say or do about you?

Depart, having received the reward of hospitality, which is the forgiveness of our death, for we do not dare to put the sword to you, we become numb, we blush at the table, we fear God, the guardian of hospitality, and we are also red with shame at the table.

It is better for us to risk our lives with Pilate, plotting against Longinus' head, than to melt our conscience and dine with the so-called bloodthirsty demons; how can our dinner be good if we bring our hands against you?
For if we do this, our hands, feet, and entire body will become numb, if we become murderers of our benefactor and host.
They were saying these things to Longinus, but they were not persuading the willing and courageous athlete to abandon the contest for the Lord and Savior Jesus Christ.
Longinus responded boldly to them, saying, 'Do not think me a traitor to life, nor a tempter of grace; may I not become a wolf in sheep's clothing; in no way will I deny what I once confessed.'

May I not lose that glory which I saw the elements trembling at, for I have witnessed the heaven covering its own appearances and the sun veiling the chariots of the lamps, the stadium of the days of light was abandoned, and night was forcibly drawn, because the weight of the cross was not endured and the blame of the Jewish god-fighting was abandoned.
How then will I scatter the wealth of so many goods given to me?
Not even the reproaches of angels will I endure.
As Longinus was still speaking, the cohort of soldiers who had been assigned to execute him arrived, having received the death sentence from Caesar.

With a cheerful face and a joyful heart, Longinus met them and kissed their eyes and neck, saying to them, 'Rejoice, fellow soldiers of Christ, conquerors of the divine contests, and heirs of the kingdom of heaven, for the gate to heaven is opening for us, and angels will receive our souls and offer them to the only-begotten Son of God.'
Behold, I see the lamps and I gaze at the crowns and I consider the prizes with which we will stand at the judgment seat of the bridegroom.
Having said these things, Longinus said to the executioners, 'If you have been ordered, make haste.'
And to the ruler of his house, he said to bring a clean robe to him, as for a wedding and a called nuptial.

Having clothed himself in the clean robe, Longinus showed with his hand the place where his blessed body was to be laid, and bending his knee, he rejoiced greatly, for he had struggled through the victorious contest with his companions.
Then, his head was cut off, and he was enrolled among the choirs of apostles and martyrs, for he had shown the courage of the former and the good zeal of the latter.
The executioners took Longinus' head and offered it to Pilate, who had received money from the Jews and was doing them a favor.

When Longinus' head was brought to Jerusalem, Pilate ordered it to be shown to the Jews who thirsted for Longinus' death, and he sold the drama of the execution for a large amount of gold to those who were accustomed to buying the blood of the righteous.

Then, Pilate ordered Longinus' precious and fearful head to be thrown away outside the gate of the city, where it lay like an untouchable treasure, preserved unharmed despite the filth that surrounded it.

A widow from the Cappadocian region, having cast away the eyes of her body, overcame her physical limitations by faith, and with her only child, she traveled to Jerusalem, where she hoped to regain her sight by venerating the holy places.
As she was led by her child, she would gather the dust of the earth and examine it with her own eyes.

The translation aims to preserve the original word order and meaning as much as possible, while still producing natural literary prose.
No obvious Bible references were found in this passage beyond the noted allusions.

title: Consolation in Faith
english: ...She hoped to soothe him, perhaps seeking to find the eye-salve in him to recover his sight, but a severe illness suddenly struck him, and he was taken from her motherly hands.
Her darkness was then doubled, and she was overwhelmed by the bitter pain of her misfortune and unceasing grief.
She cried out to God, asking how long he would neglect her until the end, and if she was being punished for her sins.
She said, 'Am I not worse than the prostitute whom I welcomed with myrrh for you?'
She continued, 'You have deprived me of both the light and my only son; and for me, there is no longer any hope of salvation.'
Longinus, the centurion who had confessed Jesus as the Son of God, appeared to her in a dream.
He told her about his own beheading and the fate of his body, which had been thrown outside the city by the Jews who had bought it through lying accusations against him.
Then I will present to you the child with glory, who will comfort your sorrow.
The woman was comforted by these words, and with newfound bravery and faith, she hastened to the task at hand.
Having learned from her faithful guides that a mound of dung had been heaped up in that place, she hastened to the place where they had led her and began to dig with her own hands.
By God's providence, she quickly uncovered the precious head, and immediately she saw the sun's rays.
Having wrapped and washed it with all haste and anointed it with precious oils, she returned carrying the pearl to where she had lodged.
The next night, the blessed Longinus appeared to her, holding her son by his side, shining and smiling, and dressed like a bridegroom.

Longinus spoke to the woman, saying, 'Behold, the one you have longed for is here. This is the one you thought was snatched from your hands. But God, having freed him, has enlisted him in the kingdom above. And now I have him with me; for I received him from the Savior, and he will never depart from my right hand. Having taken my head and your child's body, place them in one coffin, and no longer mourn your only child.'

For to him with me great glory has been given, and a holy altar and secret sacrifices and much-praised choirs and all-popular festivals, and many other things besides these which cannot be performed on earth, but in heaven, 'what eye has not seen and ear has not heard, nor has it entered into the heart of man' (1 Corinthians 2:9), which things God, having shown us his love towards us in deed and word, has prepared.
The mother of the young man received these words as prophetic commands and immediately rose to return to her homeland.

She took the all-honored and holy head and restored it to her own homeland, and she laid her child's relic beside the holy Longinus' shrine with joy and delight, just as the holy Longinus had commanded her.
As she did so, she proclaimed in her heart and with her tongue, knowing that to those who love God all things work together for good (Romans 8:28).

I was seeking eyes of flesh, but with them I also received the eyes of the spirit; I see the young man wearing purple, I gaze at the handsome youth; the child is star-faced and smiling at his mother and shining like a star beside Longinus' side, like the morning star beside the sun's ray, appearing many times at night and many times during the day, and not only in dreams, but also manifestly appearing to me in a manner of witnesses.

His lot is with prophets, although not having lived the life of prophets, and with Longinus he crusades, and the noble trophy of the heavenly kingdom is borne, and among angels he preaches, and in the midst of the crowd of archangels he cries out as a disciple of Longinus.
